idiom_name: DbContext + IEntityTypeConfiguration fluent mapping over POCO classes
implementation_notes: EF Core is .NET's data mapper: DbContext is at once the session, the identity map and the unit of work, entity classes are ordinary POCOs, and the object-relational correspondence is declared with the fluent API (IEntityTypeConfiguration, OnModelCreating) or data annotations. Aggregates are loaded with LINQ, mutated in memory and written by DbContext.SaveChanges, where the change tracker derives the INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements. Keep entity classes free of DbContext references and put the mapping in configuration classes so schema knowledge stays out of the domain type.
pitfalls: Change tracking means any tracked entity's property assignment is written by the next SaveChanges - an accidental mutation on a read path becomes an UPDATE unless read-only queries use AsNoTracking.
Lazy-loading proxies require virtual navigation properties, a persistence constraint that leaks into the domain type; without proxies a missing Include yields silently empty collections.
The identity map is scoped to the DbContext: a long-lived context returns stale entities and grows without bound, so one context per request/use case is the rule.
EF Core translates some expressions differently than expected (client-side evaluation, N+1 on Include chains); a query counter in tests is the practical guard.

variants.name: Dapper micro-ORM with explicit SQL mappers
variants.idiom_name: Dapper Query<T>/Execute with hand-written SQL in repository classes
variants.implementation_notes: Dapper maps a result set onto your POCOs by column name (Query<T>, Execute for writes) but deliberately ships no change tracking, identity map or lazy loading, so the mapper is the repository class you write around it: SQL string, parameter object, and the row-to-domain conversion for anything that is not a one-to-one property match. It suits query-shaped applications where the SQL matters and the object graph does not, and it keeps the domain type completely free of persistence attributes.
pitfalls: Column-to-property matching is silent: a renamed column leaves the property at its default value, so assert the returned shape or select explicit aliases.
Without an identity map, two queries for the same row produce two objects; de-duplicate in the mapper or add a session-scoped cache.
Dapper caches query plans in a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by SQL text - dynamically composed SQL grows that cache without bound.
